_comment: DRAFT species list for UK and Ireland waters. Names, identification features, and lookalikes must be checked by the King's biology department before launch. Conservation status is deliberately left out until it has been verified from a current source (eg the IUCN Red List).

groups.name: Catsharks (spotted, on the seabed)
groups.hint: Small, slim, spotted sharks that rest on the seabed. The most common sighting for divers.
groups.question: Which catshark?

groups.name: Slender, medium-sized sharks
groups.hint: Grey, streamlined sharks, often caught by anglers.
groups.question: Which slender shark?

groups.name: Large sharks of open water
groups.hint: Big, powerful sharks, usually seen from a boat or near the surface.
groups.question: Which large shark?

groups.name: Flattened sharks
groups.hint: Flat, wide sharks that lie buried in sand. They can look like a ray.
groups.question: Which flat shark?

groups.name: Rare and deep-water sharks
groups.hint: Unusual sightings. A photo is especially valuable.
groups.question: Which rare shark?

keyFeatures: Very large, often longer than the boat
Huge mouth held wide open when feeding at the surface
Very long gill slits that almost circle the head
Often seen as a dorsal fin and tail tip moving slowly at the surface
Slim body with a bright blue back and white belly
Very long, narrow pectoral (side) fins
Long, pointed snout and large eyes
Stocky, torpedo-shaped body with a pointed snout
White patch at the back edge of the first dorsal fin
Crescent-shaped tail with two keels (ridges) on the tail stalk
Slim torpedo shape with a sharply pointed snout
Metallic blue back
Long, curved teeth visible even when the mouth is closed
No white patch on the dorsal fin (compare with porbeagle)
Upper lobe of the tail is extremely long, about as long as the rest of the body
May be seen leaping clear of the water
Slender grey shark with a long, pointed snout
Large lobe near the tip of the upper tail, which can look like a small second tail
No spots
Grey shark with small white spots scattered over the back and sides
Blunt snout and two large dorsal fins of similar size
Plain grey shark with no white spots
Blunt snout and two large dorsal fins of similar size
Slim grey shark, often with white spots along the sides
A sharp spine in front of each of the two dorsal fins
No anal fin (the small fin underneath, near the tail)
Small, usually under 1m
Covered in many small dark spots
Flaps of skin by the nostrils reach down to the mouth
Larger and stockier than the small-spotted catshark, often over 1m
Fewer, larger dark spots
Nostril flaps do NOT reach the mouth
Inside of the mouth is black
Dark saddle-shaped blotches along the back
A crest of rough scales along the upper edge of the tail
Usually found in deeper water
Flattened body with wide, wing-like pectoral fins
Gill slits on the sides of the head (on a ray they are underneath)
Often lies buried in sand with only the eyes showing
Six gill slits on each side (most sharks have five)
Only one dorsal fin, set far back near the tail
Large thorn-like scales scattered over the body
Two small dorsal fins set far back
Very large, heavy, and slow-moving
Small dorsal fins
Small parasites are often attached to the eyes
